tagline: Land of the long white cloud
overview:
New Zealand lies in the South Pacific about 2,000 kilometers southeast of Australia, far enough from anywhere that it was one of the last large landmasses humans reached. Two long islands, simply called the North Island and the South Island, plus hundreds of smaller ones, add up to roughly the area of the United Kingdom.

About 5 million people live here, and sheep outnumber them several times over. English, Māori and New Zealand Sign Language are all official. Wellington, on a windy harbor at the bottom of the North Island, is the capital and the world's southernmost capital city; Auckland, further north, is the biggest city. New Zealand is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament, and it was the first country in the world where women won the right to vote, in 1893.

The country is known for mountains, glaciers, volcanoes, rugby, and a film industry that turned its valleys into Middle-earth.
landAndNature: Because New Zealand broke away from other lands about 80 million years ago, its wildlife evolved almost without mammals, so birds took over the jobs mammals usually do. The kiwi is a shaggy, nearly wingless night bird that lays an egg about a fifth of its own weight; the kea is a mountain parrot clever enough to pick apart backpacks. The Southern Alps run the length of the South Island, topped by Aoraki / Mount Cook at 3,724 meters, with glaciers that flow down into rainforest. The North Island has active volcanoes, boiling mud pools and geysers around Rotorua and Taupō, and the country sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, so earthquakes are common. Fiordland's flooded valleys, including Milford Sound, drop straight into deep black water.
peopleAndCulture: Māori, who arrived by ocean-going canoe from Polynesia, make up about one in six New Zealanders, and Māori words, place names and ceremonies are woven into daily life. The haka, a chanted posture dance, is performed at welcomes, funerals and before rugby matches by the All Blacks, the country's famous national team. Food cooked in a hāngī, an earth oven heated with hot stones, is a feast staple. New Zealanders call themselves Kiwis and are proud of inventing bungee jumping as a commercial sport and the electric fence, and of Edmund Hillary, the beekeeper who first climbed Everest with Tenzing Norgay. Pavlova, a crisp meringue cake piled with cream and kiwifruit, is claimed by both New Zealand and Australia.
history: Polynesian voyagers settled Aotearoa around 1250–1300, becoming the Māori and organizing into iwi, or tribes. Dutch navigator Abel Tasman sighted the coast in 1642, and James Cook mapped it in 1769. British settlers, whalers and missionaries followed. In 1840 more than 500 Māori chiefs and the British Crown signed the Treaty of Waitangi, but the English and Māori versions promised different things, and disputes over land led to wars in the 1860s and huge confiscations. New Zealand became self-governing and gave women the vote in 1893. Its soldiers suffered heavy losses at Gallipoli in 1915, remembered each Anzac Day. Since the 1970s the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated treaty breaches and arranged settlements, and the Māori language has been revived in schools and broadcasting.
funFacts: New Zealand has no native land snakes, and its only native land mammals are three species of bat.
The Lord of the Rings and Hobbit films were shot across the country, and the Hobbiton movie set is still open to visitors.
Wellington is the world's southernmost capital city and one of the windiest cities on Earth.
New Zealand was the first self-governing country to give women the vote, in 1893, decades before Britain or the United States.
The kakapo, a fat flightless parrot that climbs trees and cannot fly, numbers only a couple of hundred birds.
